newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. report lists effects of air embargo on Sudan.
newsitem.headline: U.N. report lists effects of air embargo on Sudan.

text.p: A proposed U.N. Security Council ban on international flights by Sudanese aircraft could affect distribution of medicial supplies and food production in the African nation, according to a U.N. report.
But the weekend report said a flight ban would not hamper food aid from relief agencies.

The report on the possible humanitarian impact of such an air embargo was requested by the council in December, four months after it voted to impose a ban on flights abroad by Sudanese aircraft but delayed setting a date for it to go into effect.

The ban was to punish Sudan for failing to extradite to Ethiopia three men accused of trying to assassinate Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak during a visit to Addis Ababa on June 26, 1995. Sudan has said it has no trace of the wanted men.
Mandatory diplomatic sanctions and a travel ban on senior Sudanese government and army officials have been in force since last May.

The United States has been pushing for the flight ban, with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright saying last month: "We will continue to insist that Sudan desist from supporting terrorist activities and will be following up in New York to try to get additional sanctions."

The U.N. report said: "From this review, it appears that the imposition of the flight ban envisaged in SCR (Security Council Resolution) 1070 will impair the capacity of the public health authorities to facilitate patients' receiving specialised medical treatment outside the country."
It quoted Sudan's Health Ministry as saying about 3,000 patients a year were assisted with medical evacuations.
The report also said domestic air transport could be affected by a ban on flights abroad since the same airlines "rely on international access for their maintenance and economic viability."

"Considering the dependence of domestic air carriers on offshore maintenance capacities, a flight ban could have a serious impact on immunisation programmes nationwide, domestic distribution of drugs, and on food production," it said.

Regarding food relief operations in Sudan, where a civil war has long been raging, it said "It appears that emergency food assistance in government-controlled areas in the south, with the exception of Wau and Juba, does not substantially rely on domestic air transport."
Most of the food there was provided by the U.N.-coordinated Operation Lifeline Sudan and was either delivered by air from Kenya, using aircraft registered outside Sudan, or by road and river.
